standard.title: Power and authority in empire
standard.description: the experiences and perspectives of rulers and of subject peoples, and how the interaction between power and/or authority relates to the empire and/or expansion
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how power and authority operated in medieval Europe (AC9HH8K04) and the social and cultural features of the chosen empire (AC9HH8K07). They have not yet analysed the specific power structures and relationships between rulers and subject peoples in the context of empire and expansion.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the experiences and perspectives of rulers and subject peoples in the context of the chosen empire or expansion — describing how power was exercised, how authority was legitimised, how subject peoples experienced conquest or rule, and how these interactions shaped the empire's development.

nodes.label: How rulers exercised power
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how rulers in the chosen empire exercised power — including through governance systems, military force, religious authority and symbolic legitimacy — and explain how these mechanisms sustained their rule.
nodes.minimum_width: At least two mechanisms through which the chosen ruler exercised power, with a brief explanation of how they sustained authority.
nodes.typical_width: Multiple mechanisms of imperial rule. Examples: Kublai Khan as first Mongol emperor of China (Yuan Dynasty) — use of administrators from diverse backgrounds, growth of Chinese culture; the Ottoman Sultan's responsibility for justice; the millet system's governance of non-Muslim subjects; Cortés and the siege of Tenochtitlan as a display of military power transforming political authority.
wider: For the Mongols: examine the role of Marco Polo and the development of trade as evidence of how Mongol rulers used economic connections as well as military conquest to consolidate power

For the Ottomans: analyse the millet system — which regarded non-Muslim people as subjects but not subject to Muslim law — as a case study in how religious plurality was managed as a governance strategy
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how power was exercised is prerequisite to understanding how subject peoples experienced and responded to it. Students who cannot explain the mechanisms of imperial rule cannot analyse the perspectives of those ruled.

response_modes.reason: Students often conflate conquest with governance. Scaffold the distinction: how did rulers maintain power after expansion? The mechanisms of ongoing governance (administration, law, religious tolerance, trade) are different from the mechanisms of military conquest.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two mechanisms through which the chosen ruler exercised power and explains how they sustained authority
Distinguishes between how power was established (conquest) and how it was maintained (governance)

nodes.label: Experiences of subject peoples
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the experiences and perspectives of subject peoples under the chosen empire — including how conquest, governance and cultural contact affected their daily lives — and explain how these experiences differed across groups.
nodes.minimum_width: A description of the experience of at least one subject group with reference to how imperial rule affected their daily life.
nodes.typical_width: Varied experiences of subject peoples across different groups. Examples: Ottoman tolerance of Christians and Jews vs the constraints of dhimmi status; Viking attacks on monasteries (Lindisfarne 793 CE, Iona 795 CE) experienced from the monks' written perspective; Aztec subjects under Spanish conquest — introduction of disease, horses, gunpowder, loss of resources; survival of Iron Age society in early medieval Ireland transformed by Christianity, Vikings and Anglo-Norman conquest.
wider: For the Vikings: examine the written accounts of monks that contributed to the Vikings' reputation for pillaging — and question how this single-perspective source shapes historical understanding of Viking-subject encounters

For the Spanish conquest: investigate the impact of conquest on Indigenous populations (disease, horses, gunpowder, loss of natural resources) and the introduction of American crops to Europe, examining both sides of the colonial exchange

response_modes.reason: The experience of subject peoples is highly variable across empires and within them. Using multiple subject groups (e.g. Ottoman dhimmi vs Aztec commoners under Spanish rule) prevents students from generalising from a single subordinate experience.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The contrast between Ottoman religious tolerance (millet system) and Spanish colonial coercion offers rich comparative context for understanding how the ideology of empire shapes the experience of subject peoples — and why different empires produced such different outcomes for conquered populations.
success_criteria: Describes the experience of at least one subject group under the chosen empire using historically specific detail
Identifies at least one way in which the experience of different subject groups differed within the same empire

nodes.label: Interactions between power and resistance
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how subject peoples responded to imperial power — through accommodation, resistance, or cultural exchange — and explain how these interactions shaped the development of the empire or expansion.
nodes.minimum_width: At least one example of how subject peoples responded to imperial power (accommodation, resistance or exchange) with an explanation of its effect.
nodes.typical_width: Responses across accommodation, resistance and exchange. Examples: the forging of connections between Europe and Asia through Mongol trade (Marco Polo); the survival and transformation of Irish society through Viking and Norman contact; the Aztec responses to Cortés including the siege of Tenochtitlan; Viking settlements in Dublin (Ireland) and Jorvik (York) as evidence of cultural integration as well as conquest.
wider: Examine the remains of Viking settlements such as Dublin and Jorvik as archaeological evidence of cultural integration — settlements showing how 'conquerors' and 'subject peoples' created hybrid societies

For the Spanish conquest: investigate the encounters between Cortés and the Aztecs, examining how Aztec responses to Spanish power — including alliances with rival indigenous groups — shaped the outcome of the conquest

response_modes.reason: Students tend to frame subject-empire interactions as purely one-directional (conquerors act, subjects suffer). Scaffold the analysis to include how subject peoples' responses shaped the empire — trade relationships, cultural borrowing, resistance that forced governance adaptation.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one example of how subject peoples responded to imperial power
Explains how that response — accommodation, resistance or exchange — affected the development of the empire
